title: The bodhisattva ideal
hookLine: the Mahayana honors the bodhisattva who vows to help all; the two ideals are both honored in their own homes

lines: A HARE, A MONKEY KING, A PRINCE.
cards: Long before he was the Buddha, the Pali Jataka tales say, he was a hare, a monkey king, a prince who gave away everything he had. Life after life, the stories follow one being on the long road to awakening.

The Pali word for him in those lives is bodhisatta, the Buddha-to-be, and the Theravada still tells those stories in temples and at festivals. Then the Mahayana sutras take that word and open the door wide.
Not just one Buddha-to-be: anyone can take the vow and walk that road, for the sake of every living being.

teach.h: THE VOW TO FREE ALL BEINGS.
teach.b: First, the vow. In the Mahayana, a bodhisattva sets their heart on full awakening, not for themselves alone but to free all beings. That turning of the heart is called bodhicitta, the mind of awakening.
Zen students chant a set of great vows, and the first is to free beings without number. Second, the long patience.
The Indian poet-monk Shantideva wrote a line Tibetan teachers often quote: as long as space remains, and as long as beings remain, may I too remain, to ease the sorrows of the world.
Some bodhisattvas have temples and festivals of their own. Avalokiteshvara, called Guanyin in China and Kannon in Japan, hears the cries of the world; you met Guanyin in year three.
Kshitigarbha, tradition says, vowed not to rest until the hells are empty.

teach.h: TWO IDEALS IN THEIR OWN HOMES.
teach.b: Third, the two ideals in their own homes.

teach.h: THE WEEK: SHARED GROUND, TWO IDEALS.
teach.b: The Theravada centers the arahant and honors the bodhisatta path of the Buddha himself.
The Mahayana centers the bodhisattva and honors the arahants in its temple halls. Each explains its ideal in its own words, and neither needs the other to be smaller.
Fourth, the week behind us: what all share, the truths, the jewels, ethics and practice; the three turnings and their different maps; the arahant, fully freed; and now the bodhisattva.

how: Mahayana Buddhists often take bodhisattva vows and recite them in temples and retreats, and honor bodhisattvas like Guanyin with chanting and offerings; Theravada Buddhists tell the Jataka stories of the Buddha's past lives as a bodhisatta.

o: one who vows to awaken for the sake of all beings
a saint who has already left the world for good
a guardian spirit who protects a single temple

p: the mind set on awakening for all
hears the cries of the world
vowed to rest only when hells are empty

s: the word bodhisatta appears only in Mahayana texts
the Pali Jatakas use it for the Buddha in his past lives.
Shantideva wished to remain as long as beings remain, to ease the world's sorrows
as long as space remains, and as long as beings remain, may I too remain.
one ideal must be ranked above the other
each home explains its own ideal, and both are honored.

games.q: a friend from a Theravada temple and a friend from a Zen temple each describe their ideal over dinner. what do you do?
o: let each explain their own, and honor both.
say they're the same thing and change the subject.
games.why: both homes honor the other's figures in their own way: Theravada keeps the bodhisatta stories; Mahayana keeps the luohan halls.

practice: On the in-breath, bring to mind Patacara, freed, turning back to teach; on the out-breath, Guanyin, listening for the cries of the world. Let each be honored as its own home honors it, without weighing one against the other.
If one moves you more today, that's fine; keep a little room for the other.

wordCard.voice: The bodhisattva ideal. One who sets their heart on awakening for the sake of all beings: the Buddha-to-be in the Jatakas, the open vow in the Mahayana. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit bodhisattva (Pali bodhisatta): one set on awakening.

carryVoice: Your line: both honored. Two ideals, two homes, and neither one made smaller. I'll be here tomorrow.
